title: Simchat Torah
hook: the reading finishes Deuteronomy and begins Genesis on the same day, with dancing
carry: finish and begin the same day

segments.voice: Yesterday, the lulav: palm, myrtle, willow and citron, bound together. Your line was every kind together.

Picture the most serious room you know, a place of quiet prayer, at its loudest. Every Torah scroll is out of the ark. People carry them in their arms like partners at a wedding, dancing in circles, singing, spilling into the street. Kids ride on shoulders waving flags. Someone's grandfather, who never dances, is dancing. A scroll gets passed to someone who's never held one. The circles go around seven times, and nobody's in a hurry. This is the last day of the fall holidays.
screen: `EVERY SCROLL OUT OF THE ARK.` → `DANCING WITH THE TORAH.` → `SEVEN TIMES AROUND.`

segments.voice: The day is called Simchat Torah, the joy of the Torah. It comes right after Sukkot: in Israel it's the same day as the festival called Shemini Atzeret; outside Israel it's the day after. Back on day twenty you met the scroll that never stays finished: the last lines of Deuteronomy, ending "in the sight of all Israel," and then at once, from a second scroll, "In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth." Today it happens, and the readers get honors. Their titles: the bridegroom of the Torah and the bridegroom of Genesis, and in many communities today, brides too. Then the dancing, the hakafot: seven circles around the reading table, every scroll in somebody's arms. Notice what nobody is doing. The scrolls stay closed, wrapped in their covers. No one is reading, explaining or being tested. People often point out that on this one day, the great scholar and the child who can't read a word are equal: all anyone is doing is holding the Torah and dancing. In many synagogues all the children are called up together under one big prayer shawl, spread over them like a canopy. The dancing turned up in unexpected places. In the Soviet Union in the 1960s, when religious life was pressed down hard, thousands of young Jews gathered in the street outside the Moscow synagogue on Simchat Torah night, singing and dancing. Many knew no Hebrew and none of the prayers. They knew the date. The writer Elie Wiesel went to see it and wrote about it in a book called The Jews of Silence. The joy is in holding the book, not in having mastered it.
screen: `THE BRIDEGROOMS OF TORAH AND GENESIS.` · `SEVEN CIRCLES, THE SCROLLS CLOSED.` · `THE CHILDREN UNDER ONE PRAYER SHAWL.` · `MOSCOW, THE 1960S: DANCING IN THE STREET.` · then, large: `HOLDING IT, NOT MASTERING IT.`

segments.voice: Think of something you've finished recently, a project, a season, a chapter of your life, and let it be finished. Then ask what might begin right now, and hold the end and the beginning in the same breath. Reread, or recall, the first line of something you love: a book, a song, a poem, a letter someone wrote you.
Simchat Torah. The joy of the Torah: the day the year's reading ends with Deuteronomy and begins again with Genesis, with dancing.
Your line: finish and begin the same day. The scroll never stays finished. One hundred twenty-nine days, and counting.

howItsDone: On Simchat Torah, synagogues take out all their Torah scrolls and dance with them in seven circuits called hakafot, read the end of Deuteronomy and the start of Genesis, and in many places call all the children up together under a prayer shawl.

what it means: the day the year's reading ends and begins again at once, so the Torah is never finished and put away.

what a scholar hears: a festival that grew up in the Middle Ages on Shemini Atzeret, with the hakafot added later; chatan Torah and chatan Bereshit; the Simchat Torah crowds outside the Moscow Choral Synagogue, described by Elie Wiesel in The Jews of Silence (1966).

notes: Confirm JPS 1917 wording of Deuteronomy 34:12 ending and Genesis 1:1.
Simchat Torah as a named festival developed in the geonic/medieval period; hakafot with all scrolls are later (16th century onward). Confirm the trapdoor wording.
'Brides of the Torah' in many non-Orthodox and some Orthodox women's settings; phrased 'in many communities today'.
Lamed-bet = lev: a popular homiletic teaching, not a classical source. Confirm it's acceptable to present as 'rabbis like to point out'.
Kol ha-ne'arim (children under one tallit): widespread custom; confirm.

Rewritten to pick up day 20 in one line and add new material: the hakafot with closed scrolls (no one reading, scholar and child equal), and Soviet Jews dancing outside the Moscow synagogue on Simchat Torah in the 1960s. Teach heads, match, myth and trapdoor updated; the 'lev' item removed (the note above about it no longer applies).

Confirm: Moscow Simchat Torah street gatherings in the 1960s ('thousands of young Jews', many without Hebrew) and Elie Wiesel's account in The Jews of Silence (1966); confirm the 'scholar and child are equal because the scrolls stay closed' line is fair to present as a common teaching.
